presenterNotes: Block 1: Emphasize the five steps for constructing a frequency distribution. Use the GPS navigator example to show the power of grouping.
Block 2: Walk through the formulas for midpoint, relative frequency, and cumulative frequency. The expanded table is a great visual summary.
Block 3: Make sure students understand why class boundaries are needed and how they differ from limits. Draw a quick sketch of a histogram.
Block 4: Highlight the differences among the four graph types. The ogive is often the trickiest; use the GPS example to show how to read cumulative information.
Block 5: The blueprint ties everything together. Use a fresh small dataset and model the entire process from start to finish.

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine you're a product analyst reviewing 30 GPS navigator prices. Listing them all gives you a headache. But grouping them into price ranges and counting how many fall into each range reveals the story instantly — which price range is most popular, and how prices are spread. This grouping is called a frequency distribution.

blocks.title: Constructing a Frequency Distribution
teacherCues: Show a list of 30 GPS prices and ask: 'How can we organize these numbers to see patterns?'
Write on the board: 'Class width = (max – min) / #classes, then round UP.'

explanation: A [[kw:frequency distribution]] is a table that shows [[imp:classes (intervals) of data]] with a count of the number of entries in each class. The count is the [[kw:frequency]] $ f $.
Each class has a [[kw:lower class limit]] (smallest value) and an [[kw:upper class limit]] (largest value). The [[kw:class width]] is the difference between consecutive lower limits.
The [[kw:range]] of the data is $ \text{max} - \text{min} $. To find the class width, divide the range by the desired number of classes (usually 5–20) and [[imp:round up]].
Constructing a frequency distribution: 1) Decide number of classes. 2) Find class width. 3) Set class limits (no gaps, no overlaps). 4) Tally data entries. 5) Count frequencies.

legend.meaning: Always round up to the next convenient number, even if the division gives a whole number.

examples.prompt: GPS prices (in dollars): min = $ \$59 $, max = $ \$450 $. Use 7 classes. Find the class width.
examples.title: Example A – Finding Class Width
steps: Compute range: $ 450 - 59 = 391 $.
Divide by number of classes: $ 391 / 7 \approx 55.86 $.
Round up to the next convenient number: class width = $ 56 $.
The first lower limit can be the minimum, $ 59 $.
First lower limit = $ 59 $. Next lower limit = $ 59 + 56 = 115 $.
Upper limit of first class must be one less than the next lower limit to avoid overlap: $ 115 - 1 = 114 $.
Continue adding $ 56 $ to get lower limits: $ 171, 227, 283, 339, 395 $.
Upper limits are one less than the next lower limit; last upper limit = $ 395 + 56 - 1 = 450 $ (or min + width).

Explain to a partner: Why is the upper limit of the first class $114$ and not $115$?

steps: Class 115–170 includes 130, 150.
Class 171–226 includes 200.
Class 227–282 includes 250.

confusionCorner.title: Class Limits vs. Class Boundaries
confusionCorner.body: Class limits are the smallest and largest data values that can go into a class. Class boundaries are used later for histograms and are halfway points between limits (e.g., $ 114.5 $ between 114 and 115). [[imp:Limits are for the table; boundaries are for graphs.]]

blocks.title: Expanding the Frequency Distribution

discoveryHook.scenario: A basic frequency table counts how many GPS units fall into each price range. But we can add three more columns that reveal even more: the midpoint (a representative value), the relative frequency (what fraction of the total), and the cumulative frequency (how many fall below each upper boundary). These extras turn a simple count into a powerful summary.

confusionCorner.title: Relative vs. Cumulative Frequency
confusionCorner.body: Relative frequency tells you what fraction of the whole data set falls in a single class. Cumulative frequency tells you how many data values are less than or equal to the upper boundary. [[imp:Don't mix them up!]] Relative = part/whole; cumulative = running total.

teacherCues: Ask: 'What's the middle value of the first class?' and introduce midpoint.
Show a complete expanded table and ask: 'What's the difference between relative frequency and cumulative frequency?'

examples.prompt: For the first class 59–114 with $ f = 5 $ and $ n = 30 $, find the midpoint, relative frequency, and cumulative frequency.
examples.title: Example A – Finding Midpoint, Relative & Cumulative Frequency
steps: Relative frequency: $ 5 / 30 \approx 0.17 $ (or 17%).
Cumulative frequency: first class, so it's just $ 5 $.

examples.prompt: For class 115–170 ($ f = 8 $), its midpoint is $ 142.5 $ and relative frequency $ 0.27 $. Explain how to get the cumulative frequency.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why is the cumulative frequency of the second class $ 13 $ and not just $ 8 $?
steps: Cumulative frequency adds the current class frequency to all previous frequencies.
Previous cumulative was $ 5 $, so $ 5 + 8 = 13 $.
This means 13 GPS units are priced at or below $ 170.50 $ (upper boundary).
examples.title: Example B – Continuing the Pattern
Example C – Checking the Sum
examples.prompt: If relative frequencies for 7 classes are 0.17, 0.27, 0.20, 0.17, 0.07, 0.03, 0.10, what should they approximately add to?
steps: Due to rounding, the sum of relative frequencies should be about $ 1 $ (or 100%).
Here, $ 1.01 $ is acceptable.

explanation: The [[kw:midpoint]] of a class is the average of its lower and upper limits: $ (\text{Lower} + \text{Upper}) / 2 $. It serves as a representative value for the class.
The [[kw:relative frequency]] is the proportion of data in a class: $ \text{Frequency} / n $, where $ n $ is the total sample size. It can be a fraction, decimal, or percent.
The [[kw:cumulative frequency]] is the sum of the frequencies of that class and all previous classes. The last cumulative frequency equals $ n $.
Adding these columns to the frequency distribution creates an [[imp:expanded frequency distribution]].

Explain to a partner: If bars don't touch, what false impression does it give about the data?
steps: Quantitative data are continuous; there are no gaps between possible values.
Gaps would suggest that no prices exist between classes, which is false.
Using boundaries ensures bars touch, reflecting the continuous nature.
examples.prompt: Without boundaries, a histogram of the GPS data would have gaps between bars. Explain to a partner why that misrepresents the data.

steps: Label horizontal axis with class boundaries (e.g., 58.5, 114.5, ...).
Label vertical axis with frequencies (0 to 8).
For each class, draw a bar from lower to upper boundary with height equal to frequency.
The bars should touch; the histogram shows the highest frequency in the $115–$170 range.
examples.title: Example C – Drawing a Histogram
examples.prompt: Using the boundaries from the table, sketch a histogram for the GPS frequency distribution.

legend.meaning: subtract 0.5 from lower, add 0.5 to upper to eliminate gaps between bars.

explanation: A [[kw:frequency histogram]] is a bar graph where the horizontal axis is quantitative (the data values) and the vertical axis shows frequencies.
Consecutive bars must [[imp:touch]] because the data are continuous; there are no gaps between classes.
To make bars touch, we use [[kw:class boundaries]] instead of limits. For integer data, lower boundary = lower limit − 0.5, upper boundary = upper limit + 0.5.
The height of each bar equals the class frequency.

confusionCorner.title: Histogram ≠ Bar Graph
confusionCorner.body: In a regular bar graph, bars are separated because categories are distinct (e.g., car brands). In a histogram, bars touch because the data are continuous. [[imp:Always check whether the horizontal axis is categorical (gap) or numerical (touch).]]

discoveryHook.scenario: A frequency table is helpful, but a picture is worth a thousand numbers. A frequency histogram transforms the classes and frequencies into bars that touch, instantly revealing the shape of the distribution — where data clump together and where they spread out.

blocks.title: Frequency Polygons, Relative Frequency Histograms, and Ogives

legend.meaning: Choose based on what you need: trend (polygon), proportion (relative histogram), or accumulation (ogive).

formulaCard.title: Graph Types at a Glance
formulaCard.formula: $$\begin{array}{ll} \text{Frequency Polygon} & \text{midpoint vs. } f \\ \text{Relative Freq. Histogram} & \text{boundaries vs. } f/n \\ \text{Ogive} & \text{upper boundary vs. cumulative } f \end{array}$$

explanation: A [[kw:frequency polygon]] is a line graph that plots each class's frequency at its midpoint, then connects the dots. Extend the line to the horizontal axis before the first and after the last class.
A [[kw:relative frequency histogram]] has the same shape as a frequency histogram, but the vertical axis shows relative frequencies (decimals or percentages) instead of counts.
An [[kw:ogive]] (pronounced o-jive) is a line graph that plots the cumulative frequency at each upper class boundary. It always slopes upward and ends at $ n $.
The ogive's steepest section shows where the greatest increase in cumulative frequency occurs, which is the class with the highest frequency.

confusionCorner.title: Frequency Polygon vs. Ogive
confusionCorner.body: Both are line graphs, but a frequency polygon uses midpoints and shows individual class frequencies. An ogive uses upper boundaries and shows accumulating totals. [[imp:Frequency polygon goes up and down; ogive only goes up.]]

teacherCues: Draw a frequency polygon on top of a histogram. Ask: 'What does the line show that the bars obscure?'
Show an ogive and ask: 'If I want to know how many cost $300 or less, which graph helps?'

discoveryHook.scenario: The histogram is just the beginning. A frequency polygon connects the midpoints, highlighting the overall trend. A relative frequency histogram lets you compare proportions across different data sets. And an ogive (cumulative frequency graph) answers 'how many are below' questions instantly. Each graph tells a different part of the story.

examples.title: Example A – Building a Frequency Polygon
examples.prompt: Using the GPS data, plot the frequency polygon. Midpoints: 86.5, 142.5, 198.5, 254.5, 310.5, 366.5, 422.5. Frequencies: 5, 8, 6, 5, 2, 1, 3.
steps: Plot the seven points (midpoint, frequency).
Connect them with straight lines.
Extend the line left to midpoint $ 30.5 $ (one width below 86.5) at frequency 0.
Extend right to midpoint $ 478.5 $ (one width above 422.5) at frequency 0.
The polygon shows a peak at $ 142.5 $ and then a decline.

Go up to the line, then left to the cumulative frequency axis.

examples.title: Example C – Relative Frequency Histogram
examples.prompt: Convert the GPS frequency histogram to a relative frequency histogram. The class 115–170 has frequency 8 out of 30. What is the bar height?
steps: Relative frequency = $ 8 / 30 \approx 0.27 $.
The vertical scale now goes from 0 to 0.30 or so.
Draw bars with the same class boundaries, heights = relative frequencies.
Shape is identical to the frequency histogram; only the y-axis labels change.

examples.title: Example A – Full Blueprint
steps: Understand: Min=55, Max=95, Range=40. Choose 5 classes. Class width = ⌈40/5⌉ = 8.

Solve: Limits: 55–62, 63–70, 71–78, 79–86, 87–94 (and 95? adjust). Let's use 55–62, 63–70, 71–78, 79–86, 87–94, and 95–102 if needed. We'll recalc width: 95–55=40, 40/5=8, round up? 8. Limits: 55–62, 63–70, 71–78, 79–86, 87–94. But 95 is outside; better to start at 55 and width 9? We'll adapt: use min 55, width 9 gives limits 55–63, 64–72, 73–81, 82–90, 91–99. That covers up to 95. Tallying gives frequencies 4, 5, 5, 4, 2. Frequencies sum to 20.
Solve – Table: add midpoints (59, 68, 77, 86, 95), relative frequencies (0.20, 0.25, 0.25, 0.20, 0.10), cumulative (4,9,14,18,20).
Solve – Graph: Histogram with boundaries 54.5–63.5, 63.5–72.5, etc. Frequency polygon with midpoints.
Conclude: The distribution peaks in the middle two classes (64–72 and 73–81) and is roughly symmetric. About 70% of scores are below 81.5 (cumulative 14/20).

examples.prompt: A manager wants to know what fraction of monthly sales are below $5000. Which graph would you show?
steps: An ogive (cumulative frequency graph) directly shows the number or proportion below any value on the horizontal axis.
A histogram requires adding bar areas, which is less precise.
Therefore, the ogive is the best choice for this question.

examples.title: Example C – Your Turn: Small Dataset
examples.prompt: Use the blueprint on these data (n=15): 12, 15, 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25, 28, 30, 32, 35, 38, 40, 42. Choose 5 classes.
steps: Understand: min=12, max=42, range=30. Width = 30/5 = 6 → 6.

Solve: Limits: 12–17, 18–23, 24–29, 30–35, 36–41 (and 42? adjust). Actually 42 would be in next class. To include 42, make last class 36–42 if width 7? Better to start at 12 with width 7: 12–18, 19–25, 26–32, 33–39, 40–46. Then 42 fits. Tally and compute frequencies.
Conclude: The distribution appears somewhat uniform or slightly right-skewed.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Build a Frequency Distribution and Graph

confusionCorner.body: When the maximum data value doesn't fit neatly into the last class, adjust the starting lower limit or the width slightly. The guidelines are flexible; the goal is that every data point falls into exactly one class. [[imp:Classes must cover the entire range without overlap.]]
confusionCorner.title: Fitting All Data In

legend.meaning: Turn raw data into actionable insight.

explanation: Blueprint steps: [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]].
1. [[kw:Understand]]: What data do you have? How many values? What are min, max, range? Decide number of classes (5–20).

2. [[kw:Solve]]: Compute class width (round up). Set limits and boundaries. Tally and count frequencies. Add midpoint, relative frequency, cumulative frequency. Choose the appropriate graph (histogram, polygon, ogive) based on the question.
3. [[kw:Conclude]]: Interpret the graph. Where is the center? Is the data symmetric or skewed? Which class has the most entries? What cumulative fraction lies below a certain value?

Set limits starting at min or convenient value

discoveryHook.scenario: You have a list of 20 exam scores. You need to summarize them for a report. The blueprint guides you: first understand the data, then solve by building the distribution and choosing the right graph, and finally conclude what the shape tells you. A clear method prevents mistakes and leads to insightful conclusions.
